Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II

An Operating System (OS) is system software that acts as an intermediary between
the user/application programs and the computer hardware.
It manages hardware
resources and provides a convenient and efficient environment for program execution.
Two Goals of an Operating System
1. Convenience – makes the computer system easy to use.
2. Efficiency – ensures computer hardware resources are used efficiently.
Two Views of an Operating System

• User view – OS makes the system convenient and user-friendly through interface,
performance, and ease of use.

• System view – OS acts as a resource allocator and a control program that
manages hardware and prevents errors or improper use.
Layered Structure of a Computer System

Modern operating systems are interrupt driven. Events are signaled by hardware interrupts
or software-generated traps/exceptions.

• Interrupt Vector: contains addresses of interrupt service routines indexed by inter-
rupt numbers.

• Trap (Exception): software-generated interrupt caused by an error or a user request
such as a system call.
To protect hardware from misuse, operating systems provide at least two modes.
• User mode: restricted execution; non-privileged instructions.
• Kernel mode: privileged execution; privileged instructions are allowed.
The mode bit in hardware distinguishes between user and kernel execution modes.

A timer prevents a user program from monopolizing the CPU or entering an infinite loop.

The timer generates an interrupt after a specified period, transferring control back to the
operating system.
The operating system manages several important resources.
A process is a program in execution.
• Tracks which parts of memory are in use.
• Decides which processes/data move into and out of memory.

1. User Interface – CLI, GUI, batch, touchscreen.
2. Program Execution – load, execute, and terminate programs.
3. I/O Operations – provide I/O facilities to running programs.
4. File-System Manipulation – create, delete, read, and write files/directories.
6. Error Detection – detects hardware, I/O, and program errors.

Virtualization allows multiple operating systems or execution environments to run on the
same physical hardware.

A VMM (Virtual Machine Manager) or Hypervisor creates and manages virtual
machines.
• Guest: operating system running inside a virtual machine.

Operating Systems

A process is a program in execution. A program is passive, while a process is active.
Each process is represented by a PCB.

Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II

The main goal of process scheduling is to maximize CPU utilization and provide efficient time
sharing.
• Job queue: all processes in the system.
• Ready queue: processes ready for CPU execution.
• Device queues: processes waiting for I/O devices.
• Selects a process from the ready queue.
1. Save the state of the old process into its PCB.
2. Load the state of the new process from its PCB.

Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II
A parent process can create child processes using system calls such as fork() in UNIX.
• exec() – replaces the process’s memory with a new program.
A process that has terminated but whose parent has not yet called wait().
A process whose parent terminates before the child.

Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II
In shared-memory IPC, processes communicate by reading and writing a shared memory region.

It is generally faster after setup because processes do not need kernel intervention for every
data exchange.
The producer generates data while the consumer consumes it.
A buffer is used between them.
• Unbounded buffer: no practical size limit.
Message passing allows processes to communicate without sharing the same address space.

Direct Communication
Processes explicitly identify each other.

Indirect Communication
Messages are sent through mailboxes or ports.

Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II
• Zero capacity: sender waits for receiver; rendezvous.
• Unbounded capacity: sender does not wait due to queue capacity.
Mach uses message passing extensively and provides communication through ports.
The mach_msg() function supports message communication.

Windows uses Advanced Local Procedure Calls (ALPC) for communication between local
client and server processes.
• Do not require a parent-child relationship
• Can be used by multiple processes

Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II
A thread is the basic unit of CPU utilization.
Threads belonging to the same process share:
• Concurrency: multiple tasks make progress during overlapping periods.
• Parallelism: multiple tasks execute simultaneously on multiple processing units.
• S = serial portion of the program.
• Data parallelism: same operation on different portions of data.
• Task parallelism: different tasks executed by different threads.

Operating Systems
Unit I & Unit II
Many user threads map to one kernel thread.
• Blocking system call can block entire process.
Each user thread maps to a kernel thread.

Provides greater concurrency but has greater overhead.
Examples include Linux and Windows.
Many user threads are multiplexed over multiple kernel threads.
A variation of many-to-many where a user thread may be bound to a particular kernel thread.
Pthreads is the POSIX standard API for thread creation and synchronization.
